topics.title: Variance risk premium: existence, size, index vs single stock, crash share
topics.consensus: Index option implied variance has exceeded later realized variance on average across 1986-2018+ samples, many methods and international markets: long SPX variance lost more than 50%/month in log terms (1996-2003), zero-beta SPX straddles about 3%/week, and average VIX ran 4.2 points above realized volatility in 1990-2018. The premium is much larger and more reliable for indexes than single stocks (level premium significant for only 3 of 35 stocks), mainly a correlation premium. A large, time-varying share pays for jump and crash risk and rises after crashes, so paper Sharpe ratios near 1.0-1.2 come with severe, rare losses.
topics.tier_note: A that the index VRP exists and is positive (many independent papers, US and international); A/B that the index premium exceeds the single-stock premium (direction replicated, size depends on measure and costs); B for the crash-compensation share (always large, model-dependent, no single verified percentage); C for the widely repeated '3-4 vol points' attributed to Carr-Wu (secondary only; Bondarenko's 4.2-point 1990-2018 average is the sourced figure).
topics.agreement_note: Agrees that implied usually exceeds realized and that SPX/SPY is where to harvest it; the literature frames the premium as crash insurance with fat tails, not a near-riskless statistical edge.

open_debates: Risk premium for crash, volatility and liquidity factors (Constantinides et al.; Broadie et al.) versus demand-pressure mispricing (Gârleanu et al.; Bollen-Whaley; Bondarenko's overpriced-puts puzzle).
Exploitability after costs and margin: the correlation premium is not harvestable after frictions (Driessen et al.), and margin calls cut realized Sharpe (Santa-Clara & Saretto).
Peso problem and short samples: whether 1986-2018 averages understate true crash frequency.
Which horizons are priced: only short-horizon, transitory variance appears to earn a premium (Dew-Becker et al.).
Whether the premium has shrunk since about 2016 amid crowded short-vol and 0DTE flows (suggestive index evidence only).
implications: Treat short index volatility as a real but crash-exposed premium: on paper Sharpe about 1.0 globally and above 1.2 for risk-sized 1-month SPX variance selling, with rare severe losses; put skew, max drawdown and CVaR beside win rate on the card [lit:fallon-etal-2015] [lit:fallon-park-2016] [lit:bollerslev-todorov-2011]
Use about 4 vol points as the sourced long-run index IV-RV gap (average VIX 19.3% vs 15.1% realized, 1990-2018), noting it reversed in 2008 (32.7% implied vs 35.2% realized) [lit:bondarenko-2019]

Grade single-stock premium selling well below index selling: the level variance premium was significant for only 3 of 35 stocks, and the index excess premium is correlation-risk compensation [lit:carr-wu-2009] [lit:driessen-etal-2009]

Higher dollar premium after a sell-off is not a higher risk-adjusted premium: risk-sized premia were lower after sell-offs while jump fears and tail compensation stayed elevated [lit:fallon-park-2016] [lit:todorov-2010] [lit:andersen-etal-2015]

Priced variance risk is concentrated at short horizons, so premium per unit of exposure is likely highest at short tenors (inference, not a direct 30 vs 45 DTE test) [lit:dewbecker-etal-2017] [lit:egloff-etal-2010]

topics.title: Option selling as a portfolio strategy: put-writing, covered calls, strangles and condors
topics.consensus: Systematic index option selling earns a positive volatility premium, but as a portfolio it mostly delivers lower-beta equity exposure with negative skew: PUT matched the S&P 500 over 1986-2018 (9.54% vs 9.80% CAGR) at two-thirds the volatility, while in covered calls only about 11% of premium (about 2.8%/yr) is VRP compensation. Since 2007, and especially since the 2009 trough, every Cboe short-vol index trailed the S&P 500 TR with a lower Sharpe (PUT 7.24% vs 10.95% CAGR, 2007-2026, gross), and the iron-condor index CNDR earned about 1%/yr. Paper Sharpe ratios near 2 for short strangles collapse once costs and margin calls are applied.
topics.tier_note: A that short index options earn a positive average premium; B that option-selling indexes beat equities risk-adjusted (true 1986-2018, false since 2009; mostly Cboe-sponsored studies); C that retail undefined-risk 16-delta 45 DTE strangles beat the index net of costs, margin and tails (no independent evidence; no published naked-strangle benchmark).
topics.agreement_note: Agrees that premium selling has a positive expected edge and that buying wings gives much of it back; contradicts treating the premium as the main return engine of a 25-50% sleeve, since most P&L is repackaged equity beta and results are period-sensitive.

topics.title: Protective puts and tail hedging: cost versus benefit
topics.consensus: Rolling index puts has a large, persistent cost: 1-month ATM S&P 500 puts returned -7.4%/yr excess over 1985-2018 while paying off in 8 of 8 large drawdowns, and a monthly 5% OTM overlay (PPUT) cost about 2.8-3.5 points of CAGR a year. For a given expected return, puts usually give worse drawdowns than simply holding less equity, and trend following was a cheaper crisis diversifier. The claim that small, highly convex, actively monetized hedges raise long-run compound growth rests on unaudited proprietary data from a crash-rich 2008-2020 window.
topics.tier_note: A that systematically rolled index puts lose money on average and cost more than they save in public data; B that trend following is a cheaper crisis diversifier (two related practitioner-academic studies); C that tail hedging raises long-run CAGR (press-reported, unaudited Universa claims; period-specific).
topics.agreement_note: Agrees that buying protection is a losing trade on average; nuance that holding less equity or trend beats puts, and puts still pay in sudden crashes.

topics.title: IV vs RV, IV level and rank, IV term structure and VIX futures basis as predictors
topics.consensus: Cross-sectionally, single-stock options with IV high relative to historical RV earn lower returns to buyers, and stocks with a more upward-sloping IV term structure earn higher straddle returns, so relative-value selling of rich options worked in long-short tests. For the index, evidence that high IV or high IV rank brings a better risk-adjusted short premium is weak: risk-sized SPX variance selling showed no link to IV level and lower premia after sell-offs, and VIX futures premia fall or stay flat when risk rises. The VIX term-structure slope and futures basis do predict variance and VIX-futures returns, and constant-maturity long VIX futures lost about 30%/yr in 2006-2013.
topics.tier_note: A/B for cross-sectional IV-RV and term-structure signals (top journals; long-short, cost-sensitive); B for VIX term-structure and basis predictability (several papers, mostly 2004-2015 samples, no verified post-2018 update); C for index IV-rank or IV-percentile timing (no direct peer-reviewed test; related evidence conflicts).
topics.agreement_note: Agrees with selling where IV exceeds RV in the cross-section; IV-rank timing on the index is not supported, and a 45 DTE default sits uneasily with evidence that variance risk is priced mainly at short horizons.

agreement_detail.note: Delta-hedged buyers lose more at high vol (Bakshi-Kapadia), but risk-sized returns show no IV-level link (Fallon-Park) and VIX premia fall or stay flat when risk rises (Cheng); no direct test of IV-rank thresholds.

topics.title: Earnings: implied vs realized moves, IV crush, retail buying, straddle returns and post-earnings drift
topics.consensus: Option prices reliably anticipate earnings: IV rises into the release and collapses after. Whether event options are overpriced is conditional: ATM straddles bought 3 days before announcements earned +3.34% in 1996-2010, while bellwethers, concave-IV (bimodal) names and 2021-2026 large caps show rich event options (vendor data: median implied move about 1.25x realized, held-through straddles -18.5% mean). Retail buyers into announcements lose about 5-9% on average and 10-14% around high expected-volatility events, mostly through overpaying and spreads near 20%. Post-earnings drift was large historically (about +4% over 60 days for extreme surprise deciles, 1974-1986) but is concentrated in small illiquid stocks, largely eaten by costs, and about zero for large caps since 2006.
topics.tier_note: A that IV run-up and crush exist; B/C for the sign of the earnings variance premium (contradictory, timing-sensitive); B that retail option buyers lose around announcements (one main source, consistent with Bryzgalova et al.); C for earnings straddle returns (conflicting by period, firm type and timing); A for classic PEAD historically and B for its decay since 2006; B that news-backed large moves continue while no-news moves reverse; C for the user's '>50% keep drifting over the next month' hit rate (no source reports a hit rate).
topics.agreement_note: Agrees that retail long options into earnings lose; selling into earnings is conditionally supported (large caps, modern era, realistic fills) but not universal; the user's drift hypothesis is directionally right historically but near a coin flip for large caps now.

agreement_detail.claim: Sell premium into earnings and let IV crush work
agreement_detail.note: Supported for large caps, bellwethers and concave-IV names and in 2021-2026 vendor data; contradicted by +3.34% pre-announcement straddle returns (1996-2010, smaller noisier firms) and by fat-tail moves; no peer-reviewed net-of-cost test of short strangles through earnings.

agreement_detail.claim: Buying options into earnings loses on average
agreement_detail.note: Retail losses of 5-9% (10-14% for high expected-volatility events) via overpaying and wide spreads; vendor straddles held through the crush lost 18.5% on average with a 22% win rate; exception is short pre-event windows on small firms in older data.

topics.title: 0DTE options: pricing, who trades, retail outcomes and dealer gamma
topics.consensus: SPX 0DTEs reached about 60-62% of SPX volume in 2025, with retail roughly half of 0DTE flow. They carry a positive variance premium but at same-day horizons it is small relative to spreads, estimation risk and tail losses, so the unconditional net edge is thin or absent; the one peer-reviewed paper finds 0DTEs expensive but not mispriced after costs. Retail traders, mostly buyers, lose in aggregate (press: $358k/day after daily expiries began in May 2022). Most dealer-gamma studies find 0DTE hedging dampens intraday volatility on average, while one instrumental-variable study finds a 1-SD rise in 0DTE trading raises volatility by 9.1% of its mean.
topics.tier_note: C overall (2023-2026 literature, one peer-reviewed paper, one market, about 2016-2026); C+/B- that dealer hedging dampens volatility on average (two teams converged, then merged); B- that retail buyers lose (several datasets; magnitudes vary by paper version).

topics.title: Volatility skew and put-call IV spreads as predictors
topics.consensus: In single stocks, options that are expensive on the put side predicted lower future stock returns in 1996-2012 top-journal samples: steepest-smirk stocks underperformed by 10.9%/yr risk-adjusted, expensive-call minus expensive-put stocks earned about 50 bp/week, and IV-change sorts about 1%/month. The effects shrank over time; a 2026 preprint finds the smirk insignificant in 2023-26 while the call-put spread persists, and only a few option characteristics survive firm controls. For the index, puts are clearly rich (average long-put returns about -40%/month ATM and -95% deep OTM, 1987-2000, secondary), but the skew premium is the same risk factor as the variance premium, not an extra edge.
topics.tier_note: B that single-stock skew and IV spreads predict stock returns (replicated in-sample, decaying); C+ for live implementation after costs and post-publication decay; A that index puts are rich and selling them earned a premium; C that OTM index puts are more overpriced per unit of risk than ATM.

topics.title: Trading costs and execution: spreads, fills, PFOF and margin as a cost
topics.consensus: Quoted option spreads are wide (retail-favoured weeklies average 12.6% of price), and costs plus margin cut short-option Sharpe ratios dramatically (near-maturity OTM short strangle about 1.83 to 0.16, secondary figure). Effective spreads are lower than quoted: execution-timing traders pay under 40% of conventional measures and the average trader about 75%. Mid fills are therefore attainable for patient limit orders in SPX/SPY-class liquidity but optimistic as an average assumption, and PFOF routing leaves retail option traders with less price improvement.
topics.tier_note: Graded on evidence strength because no rule text governs spreads: A that costs and margin materially reduce option-strategy returns (replicated across index and equity options, 1985-2020s, peer-reviewed); B for the size of the effective-vs-quoted gap (essentially one study, Muravyev-Pearson); B for PFOF effects on option execution (Ernst-Spatt).

topics.title: Position sizing, Kelly, risk of ruin and margin calls (Feb 2018, OptionSellers 2018, Mar 2020)
topics.consensus: Kelly sizing maximizes long-run growth only with known inputs; for negatively skewed short-option payoffs, small errors in tail estimates swing the Kelly fraction from large to zero, so fractional Kelly (0.5x or less) is the defensible practice (half Kelly keeps about 75% of growth at half the volatility). Margin rules and forced liquidation turn paper Sharpe ratios near 2 into realized ones near zero. Every documented blow-up (LJM and XIV in Feb 2018, OptionSellers in Nov 2018, Allianz Structured Alpha and Malachite in Mar 2020, Niederhoffer in 1997) combined short-vol exposure with leverage or concentration and a stated worst case far below the realized loss (LJM: 20-40% stated worst day vs more than 80% lost in two days).
topics.tier_note: A for the Kelly and fractional-Kelly mathematics (theorems plus replicated simulations); A for case-study facts from fetched SEC and CFTC documents; B for empirical short-option margin evidence (mainly Santa-Clara & Saretto through 2004 plus one 2026 Kelly put-writing study); C for any specific per-trade percentage or VIX-tiered allocation ladder (no primary source found).
topics.agreement_note: Small positions and a portfolio buying-power cap match fractional-Kelly and ruin logic; but 'trade often' diversification ignores tail correlation, and raising allocation when VIX is high coincides with margin expansion and gap risk.

agreement_detail.note: Fractional Kelly and the parameter-uncertainty argument support small sizes; but the 1-5% per-trade figure has no verified primary source.

agreement_detail.claim: Many small occurrences let results converge to the expected edge
agreement_detail.note: Averages converge only for roughly independent bets; short-vol tails are correlated, and in every case study all positions lost together.

agreement_detail.claim: Buying-power reduction is a workable unit of risk
agreement_detail.note: Portfolio margin stresses high-cap indexes only -8%/+6%, so gap losses can exceed BPR; Spina's own tables track loss-beyond-BPR probabilities.

topics.title: Management rules: profit targets, 21 DTE exits, stop-losses and rolling
topics.consensus: If option prices are close to martingales plus a risk-premium drift, exit rules cannot create edge (optional stopping); they change how long premium is held, reshape the payoff distribution and change capital turnover. tastylive's own SPY studies show 50% profit-taking raised total profit about 76% over 11 years through about twice as many trades while lowering P/L per trade, and 21 DTE exits cut the largest losses by about half. Stop-losses lower expected return under a random walk and slip in spikes, and a roll is economically a close plus a new trade.
topics.tier_note: A for the optional stopping theorem; B that management reshapes the distribution and capital efficiency (mathematically implied; consistent across vendor studies and Spina's table design); C that management raises the strategy's expected return (vendor-only, single underlying, 2005-2021, costs undisclosed).
topics.agreement_note: The 21 DTE and 50% rules are defensible as tail and capital-efficiency tools; claims that they raise edge, or that rolling lets the edge work as something other than a new trade, lack independent support.

topics.consensus: Reg T hands option margin to SEC-approved SRO rules: a naked short option needs 100% of premium plus 20% of underlying (15% for broad indexes) less the OTM amount, floor premium plus 10%, and a margin account needs $2,000. Portfolio margin revalues positions over +6%/-8% for high-cap indexes and +/-15% for equities, with a $100k regulatory minimum under full intraday monitoring (tastytrade: $125k to open, $100k to keep, house index stress -15%/+10%). Broad-based index options (SPX, XSP) and futures options are Section 1256 contracts (60/40, year-end mark-to-market, no wash sales) while SPY options are equity options; SPX/XSP are European and cash-settled. The PDT designation and $25,000 minimum were eliminated effective 4 Jun 2026 (optional phase-in to 20 Oct 2027), and IRAs bar naked puts though tastytrade's IRA The Works allows uncovered calls and futures.
